Today, we took note of the announcement by the International Committee of the Red Cross that a delegate has visited State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi in detention today in Myanmar. In accordance with the ICRC's standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty, Previously, the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General on Myanmar, Ms. Julie Bishop, has called for independent, verifiable reports on State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi's circumstances, including during her May visit to Myanmar. We welcome this development and reiterate our call for the swift and unconditional release of all those arbitrarily detained as a fundamental step towards conditions conducive to a credible transparent political process. The UN has consistently stressed that a viable political solution must be founded on an immediate cessation of violence and a genuine commitment to inclusive dialogue. The Secretary-General has stressed the importance of continued dialogue between all relevant Myanmar stakeholders and his special envoy on how the United Nations and its partners, in particular ASEAN, can help support efforts to towards a peaceful solution in the interests of the people of Myanmar, as called for by the Security Council and the General Assembly. The UN Interim Force in Lebanon continues to observe daily Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace. Between Thursday and Sunday, peacekeepers recorded 125 air violations, with a combined total overflight time exceeding 418 hours. Surveillance and armed drones were observed near or above UNIFIL positions in both sectors. Peacekeepers also report extensive military activity on the ground in South Lebanon, including significant engineering works and active troop movements. Over the weekend, peacekeepers reported multiple Israel Defence Force artillery firing events across both sectors, as well as in areas north of the Litani River. Separately, peacekeepers observed IDF activities in Lebanese territorial waters, on both Saturday and Sunday. Peacekeepers continue to face obstructions to their freedom of movement in South Lebanon. On Friday, UNIFIL patrols encountered temporary IDF roadblocks in both sectors, restricting movement in Sector East and along the coastal road in Nakoura in Sector West before access was restored. Separately, in Sector West, peacekeeping patrols were subjected to stone-throwing incidents over the weekend. Yesterday, peacekeepers discovered unexploded ordnance and improvised explosive devices in Sector East. The items were safely destroyed on site. At the request of the Lebanese Army, and following deconfliction with the IDF, a UNIFIL helicopter and personnel participated in efforts to extinguish a brush fire in the general areas of Shwaya and Ain Jarrfa, outside the mission's area of operations yesterday afternoon. On the humanitarian front, UNIFIL facilitated, in coordination with OCHA, 7 humanitarian missions in both sectors on Thursday and Friday. Turning to the occupied Palestinian territory, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says that daily airstrikes, shelling and shooting continued across Gaza over the weekend, reportedly killing dozens of people, including children and other civilians. On Saturday, one strike hit the area of Al-Aqsa Hospital, damaging an adjacent medical storage facility. The World Health Organization tells us that this caused the destruction of essential medical supplies, including some that they had delivered. Due to the proximity of the attack, the hospital building also sustained minor damage. The Ministry of Health reported that more than 150 fatalities, including dozens of civilians, were documented in July. The highest reported monthly death toll since the beginning of the year. Most strikes are being reported in western Gaza, with less than half of the Strip— within less than half of the Strip, where virtually all 2.1 million people are concentrated. OCHA stresses that under international humanitarian law, civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected and should not be targeted. Healthcare facilities must never be attacked or militarized. Further on health, our humanitarian partners warn that funding constraints continue to drive shortages of essential medical supplies, including insulin for patients with type 1 diabetes and medicines for cardiovascular diseases. Stocks of basic critical diagnostic and monitoring equipment, such as glucometers, blood glucose test strips, blood pressure monitors, and monofilaments, are also low. Affecting the quality of screening, follow-up, and disease management services. Hemodialysis services are short on key supplies, particularly vascular access supplies, while scarce quantities of cardiac catheterization materials are affecting cardiac services, squeezing treatments to a small number of priority cases. More supplies required to prevent and control infections are pending Israeli approval to bring into Gaza. Alcohol-based disinfectants, which are essential for hand hygiene and routine infection prevention, are largely unavailable. Turning to Ukraine, the Humanitarian Coordinator in the country ad interim, Auke Lutzma, today warned of escalating risks to civilians as attacks on urban areas intensify. Our colleagues from the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs tell us that over the weekend, large-scale attacks on urban centres and frontline regions killed and injured many civilians and caused widespread damage to civilian infrastructure. In the capital, Kyiv, an attack on August 1st killed at least 9 people and injured more than 30 others. The regions of Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Donetsk, Mykolaiv, Odesa, and Sumy were also heavily impacted. This is according to what authorities are telling our colleagues on the ground. Humanitarian facilities were also not spared. An attack on July 31st in the city of Pavlohrad in the Dnipro region struck a warehouse and facilities belonging to the national NGO Mission Proliska. Emergency shelter materials, clothing, and other humanitarian supplies were destroyed, including relief items supported by the UN Refugee Agency and the Ukraine Humanitarian Fund. In July alone, 4 humanitarian warehouses were hit across the country. UN agencies and partners, along with local authorities and first responders, provided emergency shelter materials, psychosocial support, and cash assistance. This past week, the Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan, together with its partners in the Quintet, the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the League of Arab States, and the European Union, continued its consultations with Sudanese political stakeholders in support of an inclusive, Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned political process. Building on the exploratory consultations held in Addis Ababa in June, the quintet engaged Sudanese civilian political leaders in recent days. They continued discussing proposals and perspectives on how to advance the political process, including through the establishment of confidence-building. Pekka Havisto, the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan, continues to engage all parties and has urged them to make concrete commitments to de-escalation and to engage in genuine dialogue towards a cessation of hostilities. Mr. Hovhannossian spoke yesterday with Sudan's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mohieddin Salan, to discuss recent developments in Sudan and prepare— and preparations for the personal envoy's upcoming visit to Khartoum. They discussed, among others, efforts to facilitate the holding of Sudanese national examinations for Sudanese students in Chad, building on the Personal Envoy's recent visit to the country. Personal Envoy Hafizto also continues to engage with General Hemeti to discuss practical measures to de-escalate the conflict. Mr. Hafizto is traveling to Türkiye this week, where he will meet with Turkish authorities as well as with Sudanese stakeholders in the country there, including youth, and women representatives. Meanwhile, our colleagues from the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs are alarmed by the deadly risks that drones are posing to civilians in Sudan. The UN Human Rights Office tells us that yesterday, a drone strike in North Darfur caused dozens of casualties. Our colleagues also note that renewed drone attacks in recent days in El Obaid and North Kordofan have put civilians critical infrastructure and humanitarian operations at risk. The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, Tom Fletcher, stressed that humanitarians are scaling up efforts to reach the families hit by the conflict in North Kordofan and will seize every opening to expand life-saving aid in and around El Obeid. He called on the parties to de-escalate, protect civilians, and ensure humanitarian access. We urge donors to increase their support for the humanitarian response. This year's appeal for Sudan is just over 40% funded, with about $1.2 billion received against the nearly $2.9 billion required. From the Democratic Republic of the Congo, our colleagues at OCHA tell us that fighting in the highlands of the province of South Kivu continues to drive people from their homes and disrupt their access to essential services. According to our humanitarian partners, clashes in the towns of Vuvira, Fizi and Mwenga have displaced more than 48,000 people since mid-July. Civilian casualties and damage to critical infrastructure were also reported. OCHA notes that insecurity, road closures, damaged infrastructure and disruptions to telecommunications are hampering humanitarian access, medical evacuations and the delivery of aid. Access to healthcare has been particularly impacted. With damage to health facilities and the departure of medical personnel limiting the availability of medical care in affected areas. These developments come as efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak continue in the province. As of August 1st, national health authorities have reported 3,748 cases confirmed— have reported 3,748 confirmed Ebola cases across Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Ouele, and Tshopo provinces. We reiterate our calls on all parties to protect civilians, facilitate safe and sustained humanitarian access, and restore telecommunications, which remain critical for civilian protection, public health efforts, and humanitarian operations. Also on Ebola in Rwanda, we, along with our humanitarian partners, continue to support government-led efforts to strengthen preparedness against the virus. Our humanitarian colleagues tell us that more than 100 personnel have been deployed to key land border crossings and airports. At points of entry, including the Rubavu and Kakitumba crossings, as well as in high-risk districts, we and our partners are helping to improve handwashing facilities, access to safe water, sanitation systems, and wastewater management. We and our partners are also supporting training at 11 health centers in the locality of Mbilisi, near the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Nearly 400 frontline personnel are receiving training in early detection, triage, infection prevention and control, waste management, safe and dignified burials, and public health messaging. Starting today until September 13th, the World Health Organization is running a global competition that calls on students and young professionals to develop videos that highlight the importance of influenza and/or COVID-19 prevention and control. The videos are encouraged to be innovative, address misinformation and myths, and encourage their community to protect themselves from seasonal influenza and COVID-19. The winning videos will be featured by WHO on the competition webpage. You can find more information on the WHO website.
